content.thinking:
I'm sketching proportions for an African bush elephant model, aiming for a shoulder height around 3.2 meters and overall body length near 3.3 meters, and starting to place the hip joint as the root of the skeleton.

I'm defining explicit body cross-section stations along the spine from rump to shoulder, specifying top/bottom heights and widths at each z-position to shape the torso profile, then starting on the skeleton hierarchy with hip and spine joints plus a tail chain.

Now I'm placing the head with a prominent domed forehead and short thick neck, then setting up leg geometry as tapered pillar columns positioned at front and hind stances, with IK targets from shoulder to foot and bent knees for the hind legs, plus rounded feet with toenails. I'm about to shape the large, Africa-shaped ears.

I'll paint the ear interior with a pinkish-grey tone and add radiating dark vein lines plus wrinkles using the surface coordinates, keeping the rim beveled with a darker edge.

For the trunk, I'll chain roughly seven joints from the head front downward using the "tentacle" role since trunk isn't a native type, tapering the sweep radius from 0.22 at the base down toward 0.1 at the tip.

Then I'll add ring-like wrinkle bands near the tip via paint on the surface coordinate, use an 8-sided low-poly profile, and set the rest pose with the trunk hanging down with a slight forward curve so the tip stays lifted about 0.25m above ground. I'll finish the tip with small dorsal and ventral lip-like spikes and a flat end cap bearing a dark nostril disc.

Writing wrinkle paint code...

I'll grab the center and tangent from the chain point rather than the sweep surface, using my radius function for sizing, and build low-poly ridge tori with minimal segments attached rigidly to that bone. For skin, I'm settling on a gray-brown elephant tone within the flat low-poly palette.

I'll layer countershading and mottling, then add a reddish-brown dust gradient along the lower legs and belly to mimic dusty soil, and tackle wrinkles using anisotropic noise lines for a cracked-skin texture.

Finishing the skin paint function... I'm also estimating texel resolution for the elephant's painted surface and considering bumping paint size to 2048 for finer detail, then thinking through how to add horizontal crease rings near the knees and ankles using a y-based wrinkle pattern.

Now I'm shifting to the head geometry, planning it as a lofted ellipsoid with a domed forehead and sloping face, defining stations from the occiput to the mouth with width and height tapering, so the trunk base connects naturally below the face.

Still defining the jaw geometry...

Mapping out the tusk curve path on each side so they sweep down then forward and up without colliding with the trunk at the center, keeping tips roughly 1.4m forward. I'm also adding a small lip ring at the tusk base and a worn gradient coloring, yellowish stain near the root fading to darker at the tip.

For the eyes, placing small amber-and-dark spheres at the sides of the head with flattened eyelid shapes and lash spikes, plus a subtle dark temporal gland stain below each eye using a distance-based paint rule.

Now I'm defining the ear shape as an outline of points in local coordinates, starting from the hinge attachment near the skull and tracing outward through bulges and curves down to a lobe point at the bottom, mapping out the ear's silhouette like a rough Africa-shaped contour.

I'm scaling the ear to realistic proportions, about 1.0 wide and 1.45 tall, then working out the orientation vectors so the ear plane flares outward and slightly backward from the head when extruded, mirroring the setup for left versus right sides.

Since mirroring just flips the geometry symmetrically, thickness should stay consistent either way. For the ear coloring, I'll paint the outer skin tone, a darker rim, and a pinkish-grey inner area near the base with subtle vein detailing, applying the paint based on whether the face normal points forward (front-facing/inner surface).

For the veins themselves, I'm thinking ridged noise patterns combined with Worley cell edges, since the thin lines between cells naturally resemble a polygon vein network. For the ear's joint structure, I'll likely keep it simple with a single hinge joint rather than a multi-joint chain, since the flop test seems fine with rigid ear parts. I'm now considering whether the body needs additional details like a head hump or back spine ridge.

Beyond that I'm adding skin wrinkle details at the shoulders and hips using dark painted creases, sparse bristle hair on the tail tip, head tuft, and chin using card geometry, plus eyelash spikes. For toenails I'm matching real elephant anatomy—four on front feet, three on hind—as flat ivory-gray wedges, and working out the foot shape as a short flattened cylinder or scaled sphere to form the rounded base.

Working out foot and nail placement...

Switching to a small 6-sided cylinder for the nail disc, oriented outward along y. Now I'm positioning these around the foot rim, figuring out the foot's geometry span and centering the nails at the right height, and attaching the foot piece to the tip joint of the leg chain so it sinks properly into the floor.

I'm now laying out the leg skeleton: shoulder, elbow/knee, and foot joints for the front legs as near-straight pillars, setting rough coordinates and limb lengths with just a slight forward bend hint to match a real elephant's stance.

Tuning the leg radius profile so it tapers smoothly from thigh to foot, with a slight bulge near the shoulder where the leg meets the body so it doesn't poke through the body surface awkwardly.

For the hind legs, I'm placing hip, knee, ankle, and foot joints to mimic a real elephant's bend — knee forward around 1.1m, hock angled back. I'm settling on three segment lengths (roughly 1.15, 0.85, 0.35) with alternating bend directions so the leg looks mostly straight with natural articulation.

Now for the body skeleton, I'm planning a spine chain running from the pelvis forward through the chest using a catmull curve, then a short neck chain connecting to a head joint, plus a tail chain extending backward from the pelvis — keeping the hierarchy simple with pelvis as root and spine/neck/tail as child chains.

Now I'm planning the tail as a thin tapering chain of four joints hanging from the rump down to a tufted end, keeping clear of the hind legs. Then I'm setting up the head joint off the neck tip, angled forward and down, followed by positioning the jaw joint beneath it.

For the jaw itself, I'm building a lower-lip wedge shape with painted detail, leaving room above for tusk sockets, and adding a small pink mouth cavity with a hint of tongue between the upper lip and jaw. I'm also shaping cheek bulges with flattened ellipsoids and adding twin forehead domes positioned symmetrically on the head bone for added facial volume.

Now I'm planning crown hair bristles, trunk wrinkle detail, and a tip structure with dorsal and ventral "finger" cones plus a recessed dark nostril disc, treating the trunk as an eight-segment tentacle chain. I'm also sketching a dust/mud gradient band to paint along the lower legs based on vertical position.

For texture detail, I want small torus rings at knee and ankle joints on each leg to suggest skin fold wrinkles, colored darker than the base skin, while skipping elbow fold lines for now.

Also planning an ear root fold at the base attachment point, plus sparse dorsal bristle tufts at the head crown, tail, and chin — rendered as thin tapered SVG strand textures.

For the eyes, I'm figuring out placement by casting a ray against the skull surface at a given height and depth, finding the hit point, then embedding a small sphere there to attach the eye naturally to the loft geometry.

Now I'm sketching out the eye detail itself: an amber sphere for the eyeball, a darker pupil offset along the normal, an upper eyelid as a scaled hemisphere, plus a lash ring made of small spikes. I'm also starting to tally up the total part count and thinking ahead to neck joints and skin fold details.

Shoulder bulges can reuse the body's skin-painted ellipsoid shapes rather than needing new flat colors, since everything shares the same paint sheet continuity. I'm listing out which parts stay flat-colored (nails, eye amber, pupil, lashes, mouth, tongue, bristle tint) versus which use the skin paint function, and starting to define the base skin color constant for that paint function.

Writing skin paint logic...

Finishing the dust-and-crease blending, I'm adding dust patches on upper surfaces too, mimicking elephants throwing dirt on their backs. I also want trunk-specific ring wrinkles using a sine pattern along the trunk's length to create periodic creases.

I'll skip torus geometry for the trunk rings and instead modulate the trunk's sweep radius with a cosine function, concentrating ridge density where the radius changes most.

Settling on 20 ridges along the trunk with 6% radius modulation, spaced evenly so none bunch together. For the ears I'll add wrinkle-noise creases in the paint, use dark skin cards for the tail tuft, then move to the mouth and jaw next. Checking proportions — head top at 3.42 and shoulder at 3.2 match real bush elephant ratios, and the ear top at 3.3 clears the head fine, so I'm confirming the overall length runs from the rump at z -1.75 to the trunk tip at z 3.1.

I'm sanity-checking the tusk curves and overall body length against real elephant measurements, then starting the actual implementation file, importing the builder, math, path, IK, and paint utilities before writing the bone chain and geometry construction code.

Writing component imports...

Now I'm setting up the root pelvis joint and spine chain structure, working through how to position the first spine joint relative to the pelvis without creating duplicate points.

Still planning the skeleton joints...

I need to make a separate head joint. For the legs, I'm figuring out parenting: hind legs attach to the pelvis, front legs attach to spine3 near the shoulder region, with the front IK root positioned off the spine's actual line.

For the body loft, I'm defining the bone chain as pelvis, spine, and neck, each owning a section of the path, with the tail chain parented to the pelvis starting near the rump. Now I'm working out the loft stations along the body, defining cross-section width and top/bottom height at each z position to shape the torso profile.

I'm checking that the leg spacing works with the body outline -- legs at 0.25 radius sitting around x=0.52-0.55, which keeps them tucked under the flank rather than flush with the body's widest point, matching how real elephants carry their legs beneath a body that's a bit wider than the stance.

For the look, I want faceted low-poly shading rather than smooth-bent surfaces, so I'm setting flat shading globally across the tubes, using fewer sides on the legs (around 8) and slightly more on the body (around 10) for the sweep geometry.

Now I'm working out the head placement and station profile, defining the joint position and forward-facing direction, then sketching cross-section stations along z with their center height, width, and height values to shape the head relative to the neck and body transition.

Continuing the loft, I'm placing the remaining stations toward the face, estimating eye position from the interpolated head width at z≈2.05, and setting eye height around 2.85. I'm also sizing the forehead and ear region, then checking how the face loft tapers down to meet the trunk base at its emergence point.

Now I'm working out the jaw geometry — joint at roughly (0,2.2,2.0) angled toward (0,2.05,2.5), with jaw stations narrowing from width 0.5 near the joint to 0.32 near the tip. I'm checking that the jaw doesn't poke through the trunk base by pulling its endpoint back to z=2.45 so it tucks behind and below where the trunk root begins, keeping it visually hidden from the front but visible from the side.

I'm thickening the trunk base to radius 0.27, placing tusk roots at (±0.22, 2.18, 2.3) tucked into the upper face with a flattened pinkish-gray lip sheath bump, and adding small dark mouth-corner boxes near (±0.2, 2.25, 2.3) in a dark brownish color to suggest the mouth slit without modeling a full interior.

Now I'm setting ear hinge joints at (±0.45, 3.1, 1.5), aiming outward with a vertical hinge axis, naming them earL/earR based on the side, and noting that eyes and other head features inherit weights from the head bone automatically.

For the feet, I'm shaping a tapered cylinder (0.25 top radius, 0.28 bottom, 0.2 height, 8 sides) centered so its bottom sits at floor level, aligning it so the IK target at y=0.17 lines up with where the limb chain ends.

Now I'm thinking about adding darker wrinkle creases on the legs using thin tori placed along the leg's sweep path, computed from the chain's parametric position and tangent at specific t-values, painted a flat dusty color to keep the palette small. I'm defining a radius function for the leg profile across t, tapering from about 0.31 at the top down to 0.225 near the knee before widening slightly toward the ankle.

Since the point from `.at` is a plain vector without bone info, I should pass `frame: cp` alongside direction and axis so positioning picks up the blended bone weighting correctly.

For the leg ridge geometry, I'm sizing the torus radius to match the octagonal cross-section's circumscribed vertices rather than its flat faces, using a thin tube with few radial segments for a faceted ridge look. Now I'm laying out the trunk joint chain parented to the head, defining the path points and radius function along its length.

Setting the trunk tip to curl slightly forward, keeping the bottom above ground level, and tapering the radius exponentially from a thick base to a narrow tip with a small flat cap for the nostril. I'm adding a cosine-based ridge pattern along the radius to mimic the trunk's natural wrinkle rings, aiming for roughly 20 rings that read well even with flat shading.

I'm setting up 8 trunk joints plus a tip, naming them trunk1 through trunk8, letting the trunk hang naturally straight in the rest pose. For the tip, I'm planning a flat cap with a darker nostril disc, and considering a small cone or capsule on top to represent the dorsal finger-like projection elephants have at the trunk's end.

Now I'm working out the geometry for that dorsal finger, computing the tangent direction at the final trunk segment and positioning a capsule extending from the top edge of the tip outward along that direction.

Normalizing gives the dorsal direction perpendicular to the tangent, which marks the back/top of the trunk. For the nostril I'm adding a small dark cylindrical disc at the trunk tip, and I'll give the ventral side lighter pink paint with fine ridges in the trunk texture. Now I'm moving on to building the tail chain.

Writing tail hair cards...

For the head, I'll scatter sparse bristle cards on the skull crown, filtering for points with a high upward normal, using tiny sizes and dark grey tinting to suggest short fuzz, leaning back slightly for flow.

Then I'm adding bristles along the trunk tip with wider spacing, and considering body creases at the shoulders and hips as draped curved sweeps to suggest skin folds, using a catmull-rom path lifted slightly and swept with a thin radius for a subtle crease line effect.

Adding sphere ellipsoids for shoulder and thigh bulges...

For the ear geometry, I need to work out which face normal counts as "front" for each ear since mirroring flips the thickness axis direction, so I'm defining the inner/outer face logic separately for left and right ears.

I'm placing the attachment edge at x=0 spanning y=0.3 to -0.6, angling the ear outward-back about 30° from the head side, with the joint near (±0.42, 3.05, 1.45). Checking the ear's vertical reach down to around y=1.6 against real elephant proportions where ears extend roughly to shoulder level, which seems about right given shoulders sit near y=3.2.

Narrowing the ear's vertical range to v=0.3 to -1.4, which puts it spanning roughly y=3.35 to 1.8. Working through the splay angle so the ear flares outward and slightly back relative to the body width, checking that at the outer edge it clears the shoulder by enough to look flared rather than pressed flat against it.

Settling on a moderate rearward flare angle for the ear so it stays close to the body without overlapping. Next I'm moving to the tusks, planning to sweep a bezier curve rigged to the head bone, tapering the radius from base to tip with ivory coloring and flat-shaded octagonal cross-sections, plus a slight tip color variation near the point.

I'm defining a color gradient for the tusks running from a yellowish-brown stained base through pale cream to a worn white tip, adding subtle grain streaks with noise for realism, then adding a pinkish-gray sheath sphere at the tusk base, and sketching out the eye using a flattened, scaled sphere embedded at a surface hit point with a smaller pupil sphere nested inside.

Now I'm working out eyelids using a thin rotated torus ring around each eye, plus lashes placed in an upper arc around the eye using angle-based ring placement with outward-tilted spikes.

Then I'm adding twin forehead domes as scaled spheres on the head stick, skin-painted, and figuring out cheek/temporal wrinkles by checking proximity to the eye positions in the paint logic.

I'm computing a streak factor using distance from the eye z-position and x-threshold to create dark tear-stain marks below the eyes within a bounded y-range. Next I'm checking the paint shader's performance for cells and noise per texel, then starting on the leg dust gradient rising from the ground.

The feet should be almost entirely covered in dust, and the trunk/head skin gradient should stay smoother and lighter lower down. For the mouth, I'll skip deep detailing and instead add small dark pinkish ellipsoids at the jaw hinge corners on each side, scaled and positioned near the existing jaw joint, while skipping the tongue and chin hairs for simplicity. I'm roughly tallying part counts now: body loft, head, jaw, and four legs each with several joint rings, adding up the total.

Counting through the remaining components—toruses, feet, nails, tusks, sheaths, eyes with lashes, trunk ridges, tip, ears with rims, tail, and bulges—I land on roughly 120 parts total, which feels reasonable for an animal model even if "few hundred parts" is more typical for full dioramas. I want to add more richness: wrinkle ridges at the hips and shoulders, trunk-side hair, foot toe detail, and possibly ear veins as raised ridges, though painting veins directly might suffice instead of modeling them. I'm considering sweeping a thickened rim along the ear outline using a closed polyline sweep for extra edge definition.

I can map the ear outline points through the ear part's local transform to get proper world coordinates for the rim sweep, using a slightly thicker, darker-colored radius so the scalloped edge reads clearly, and I like the idea of adding a small tear or notch in the lower edge for character. I'm also planning sparse dark hair cards scattered across the back where the surface normal points upward, plus a few thin horizontal wrinkle rings around the barrel of the body at different z-positions to suggest subtle fold lines in the elephant's hide.

I need to be careful choosing those z positions so the rings land on the torso and don't accidentally slice through the legs, then move on to adding mud splotches and similar skin paint details, being mindful of unused parameters in the paint closures.

For the legs I'm adding wrinkle creases driven by sine waves and noise, restricted to the lower portion since the tops are hidden under the body. Then I move to handling the eyes, surfacing the skull loft and raycasting onto it to place them correctly.

I'm checking the tail chain setup and confirming the pose stays at rest with no bending applied yet. For the hind limb, I'm computing root and target positions and noticing the segment lengths sum close to the actual distance, meaning the leg would render nearly straight—so I need to adjust the lengths to allow for proper bending.

Increasing segment lengths to create a visible knee bend, then setting up the front leg similarly with a slight forward curve and naming the joints shoulder, elbow, and hand. I'm also defining side naming conventions (L/R) and working out a radius function for leg thickness that tapers along the limb.

Hind legs get a thicker taper, and I'm defining the foot as a short tapered cylinder with flat shading that nestles into the leg's end cap, plus setting up nail placement around the foot's edge (four front, three hind).

For nail bone binding, I want to lean on the ring's literal line to find the nearest joint automatically rather than forcing it to the tip bone, since passing an explicit bone through the ring callback might fight with how the system infers nearest-bone attachment at the foot's base.

Explicit bone references to leg.tip should work fine, with the foot rigid at the tip joint while the leg tube itself stays smoothly skinned across the joint. I still need to handle toes for the hind legs similarly.

For the ears, I'm setting up a hinge joint parented to the head with a specified direction, then extruding the ear shape from that joint with a thin thickness and perpendicular up-vector, using bevel and smoothing for a natural look. Now I'm working out the ear's outline coordinates relative to its attachment point.

Still writing outline points...

For the rim, I'm sweeping a closed catmull curve through the ear outline points, offset slightly inward to account for corner rounding, with a small radius and darker color to define the ear's edge.

For the ear paint, I'm defining a shader that adds a pinkish front face plus a network of vein-like cell lines, working in model space coordinates that differ slightly between left and right ears but still work correctly.

Now I'm classifying ear surfaces by normal direction: front when the z-normal exceeds 0.15, back when it's below -0.15, and rim otherwise since the edge walls are thin anyway. I also need to set body lofts with flat shading and no smoothing, position the loft stations at the midpoint between top and bottom, treat the neck as essentially part of the head/hump bone chain, and add some skin fold loops before moving on to the tail.

Writing tail tuft texture...
